concepts.name: Government, its functions and the idea of representation
concepts.description: The roles of government, the school committee example, representatives and the legislative, executive and judicial functions.
concepts.idea: A government makes rules, implements them and ensures they are followed, and democracies choose representatives to do so.
concepts.rule: A government maintains law and order, ensures peace and security, manages relations with other countries, takes care of defence, delivers goods and services, manages the economy and works for welfare. The school example shows three ways to form a student committee: everyone joins, the Head Teacher chooses, or students elect representatives. Electing representatives is the democratic way. A representative acts on behalf of a group. Making rules is the legislative function, implementing them is the executive function and ensuring they are followed is the judicial function. Democracy means rule of the people.
concepts.example: Lincoln described democracy as government of the people, by the people, for the people.

questions.q: A well-known description of democracy is 'government of the people, by the people, for the people'. This phrase is attributed to
questions.a: Abraham Lincoln, a President of the United States
o: Abraham Lincoln, a President of the United States
Mahatma Gandhi, in the context of the Indian republic
Montesquieu, in his work on the separation of powers
B. R. Ambedkar, in his speech closing the Constituent Assembly debates
questions.e: Abraham Lincoln, a U.S. president, described democracy in this way in his Gettysburg Address; the phrase is still widely used.
w: Rejected: the phrase is attributed to Lincoln, not to Gandhi.
Rejected: Montesquieu is linked with the separation of powers, not this phrase.
Rejected: Ambedkar is associated with the idea of social democracy, not this phrase.

w: Rejected: this is the objection to the first method, where every student is on the committee.
Rejected: no such objection is made against the second method.

questions.q: A State legislature lays down that no vehicle may carry more than a stated load on rural roads; the State transport department puts this rule into practice; a court hears the case against owners who flout it and penalises them. questions.a: the legislative, the executive and the judicial function

the judicial, the executive and the legislative function

questions.e: Creating rules is the legislative function, implementing them and administering the country by them is the executive function, and ensuring that they are followed is the judicial function; a court that hears a case and penalises those who break the rule performs that last function.
w: Rejected: it swaps rule-making and rule-implementation.
Rejected: it places the judicial function first, though a rule must exist before it can be enforced or implemented.
Rejected: it swaps implementation and ensuring that rules are followed.

questions.q: Which thinker, in which work, put forward the doctrine that concentration of powers in one person or body leads to despotism, in order to promote individual liberty?

concepts.name: What makes governments different, and the principles of democracy
concepts.description: Four key differences between governments and the fundamental principles of democracy.
concepts.idea: Governments differ in who gives authority, how they form, their parts and their goals; democracies share equality, freedom and representation.
concepts.rule: Four questions distinguish governments: who decides that this is the government; how the government is formed; what its parts are and what they do; and what it is working for. In a democracy the people are the source of authority, in a theocracy religious belief and the head of a religious institution. Democracy's principles are equality, freedom, representative participation, universal adult franchise, fundamental rights and an independent judiciary. India gave universal adult franchise from 1950; Swiss women got the vote only in 1971.
concepts.example: In a monarchy someone from within the family usually continues to rule.

questions.q: Forms of government can be distinguished on four major aspects. Which one of the following is NOT one of those aspects?
questions.a: How large the population of the country is
o: How large the population of the country is
Who decides that 'this is the government'
What the different parts of the government are and what they do
What the government is working for and what goals it tries to achieve
questions.e: The four aspects are who decides that this is the government, how it is formed, what its parts are and what they do, and what it is working for. Population size is not among them.
w: Rejected: this is the first aspect.
Rejected: this is the third aspect.
Rejected: this is the fourth aspect.

questions.q: A country's government derives its authority from religious beliefs and from the head of a religious institution rather than from the people. In the classification of governments, this government is best described as a
questions.e: In a theocracy the source of authority is religious beliefs and the head of a religious institution, whereas in a democracy like India it is the people. A constitutional monarchy has real power in an elected government; an oligarchy is rule by a small group of wealthy families or influential people.
w: Rejected: in a constitutional monarchy real executive power lies with the prime minister and an elected parliament.
Rejected: an oligarchy is rule by a small group, usually wealthy families or influential people.
Rejected: in a representative democracy the people elect those who govern them.

questions.q: Which one of the following is NOT a Fundamental Right guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution at present?
o: The right to freedom of speech and expression
questions.e: The right to property was removed from Part III by the 44th Amendment (1978) and is now only a legal right under Article 300-A. The rights to equality, to freedom of speech and expression, and against exploitation remain Fundamental Rights.
w: Rejected: the right to equality is a Fundamental Right (Articles 14-18).
Rejected: freedom of speech and expression is a Fundamental Right (Article 19(1)(a)).
Rejected: the right against exploitation is a Fundamental Right (Articles 23-24).

questions.q: 'Independent judiciary' is among the fundamental principles of democracy. Which one of the following is the role of such a judiciary?
questions.a: Ensuring that citizens' fundamental rights are protected and that laws are followed by citizens as well as by all parts of the government
o: Ensuring that citizens' fundamental rights are protected and that laws are followed by citizens as well as by all parts of the government
Making the laws that serve as the framework for running the country, in consultation with the elected representatives of the people
Choosing the representatives who sit in the legislature through a process of regular and fixed elections held every few years
Deciding the goals the government should work towards, such as equality and prosperity for all citizens of the country
questions.e: An independent judiciary ensures that every citizen's fundamental rights are protected and that laws are followed by the citizens and also by all the parts of the government.
w: Rejected: making laws is the legislative function.
Rejected: representatives are chosen by the people through elections.
Rejected: the goals a government works for are part of its design, not a judicial role.

questions.q: Which one of the following correctly compares the spread of universal adult franchise in India and Switzerland?
questions.a: India provided it from the beginning of the republic in 1950, whereas Swiss women got the vote only in 1971
o: India provided it from the beginning of the republic in 1950, whereas Swiss women got the vote only in 1971
India provided it from the beginning of the republic in 1950, whereas Swiss women had got the vote in 1928
India provided it only after Swiss women had won the vote in 1945, a few years before the Indian republic began
Switzerland gave every adult the vote when it became a democracy in 1848, whereas India did so only in 1971
questions.e: India provided universal adult franchise from the very beginning of the republic in 1950; in Switzerland women got the right to vote at the federal level only in 1971. Years such as 1928 (Britain) and 1945 (France) belong to other countries.
w: Rejected: 1928 is the year Britain gave women equal franchise; Swiss women got the vote in 1971.
Rejected: 1945 is the year France gave women the vote; Swiss women voted only in 1971, long after the Indian republic began in 1950.
Rejected: 1848 is the year the modern Swiss federal state was founded, not the year of women's vote; India's adult franchise dates from 1950.

concepts.name: Direct and representative democracy, parliamentary and presidential
concepts.description: Direct and representative democracy, accountability, elections and the two forms of representative democracy.
concepts.idea: Most democracies are representative, either parliamentary (like India) or presidential (like the USA).
concepts.rule: In a direct democracy all citizens take part in every decision, as in a form followed in Switzerland; it is hard in large countries. In a representative democracy people elect representatives by universal adult franchise and the government is accountable to them, with elections at fixed intervals: every five years in India, every four in the USA. In a parliamentary democracy the executive is part of the legislature and works while it has the confidence of the Lok Sabha; people elect the legislature, not the executive. In a presidential democracy the executive works independently of the legislature and the president is elected by the people. Most legislatures have an Upper and a Lower House.

concepts.name: Early republics and kingship in India
concepts.description: Republics such as Vajji and the Lichchhavis, the Uttaramerur elections, republics elsewhere, and rajadharma.
concepts.idea: Ancient India had republics and elections, and even kings were expected to follow rajadharma.
concepts.rule: A republic is a government whose head of state is elected and not a hereditary monarch. In the Vajji mahajanapada the Lichchhavi clan practised collective decision-making and leaders were chosen by merit. The Uttaramerur inscriptions of the 10th century CE in Tamil Nadu describe the election of members to the village sabha, with sealed ballot boxes, qualifications, duties and grounds for dismissal; a corrupt member was removed at once. Rome and Greece had republics in the 5th and 4th centuries BCE but not everyone could vote. The power of the raja was not absolute; he had to follow rajadharma, ruling by dharma for the welfare of all.
concepts.example: Bhishma taught Yudhishthira that a raja's authority is temporary and bound by dharma.

concepts.name: Monarchies today and theocracy
concepts.description: Absolute and constitutional monarchies and theocracies with examples.
concepts.idea: In an absolute monarchy the monarch holds all power, in a constitutional monarchy real power lies with an elected government.
concepts.rule: A monarchy is ruled by a monarch, a king or queen, usually hereditary, who exercises sovereign power. In an absolute monarchy the monarch controls making, enforcing and adjudicating laws; Saudi Arabia is an example, where the king governs by Islamic law and appoints a council he need not follow. In a constitutional monarchy, such as the United Kingdom, the monarch has only nominal power, the prime minister exercises executive power and the elected parliament makes laws. A theocracy is ruled by religion and religious leaders; Iran combines theocratic and democratic elements with a Supreme Leader selected by clerics for life. Others are Afghanistan and Vatican City.
concepts.example: The UK has a king but is really a parliamentary democracy.

concepts.name: Dictatorship and oligarchy
concepts.description: One-person rule, examples such as Hitler and Idi Amin, life under strict control and rule by a few.
concepts.idea: In dictatorships and oligarchies power is held by one person or a small group without real limits.
concepts.rule: A dictatorship is a government in which one person or a small group holds absolute power with no limits from a constitution or law. Adolf Hitler, appointed Chancellor of Germany in 1933, passed laws giving himself full power and eliminated opposition; he was responsible for the Holocaust, at least six million Jews killed, and caused World War II (1939-1945). Idi Amin was a military dictator in Uganda who killed thousands and forced many Indians to flee. An oligarchy, from the Greek olígos (few) and árkhō (to rule), is rule by a small powerful group, usually wealthy families or influential people; some democracies show signs of oligarchy.

concepts.name: Why democracy matters, and its challenges
concepts.description: Comparing forms of government, benefits of democracy and the problems democracies face.
concepts.idea: Democracy gives people rights and a say, but citizens must stay vigilant against its problems.
concepts.rule: In a democracy the people choose their government, which is accountable for protecting rights and providing basic needs; if it fails, people can change their representatives through elections. People can choose what to speak, wear and believe as long as they do not harm others' rights. Universal adult franchise exists in democracy but not in dictatorship, absolute monarchy or oligarchy. More than half of the world's countries have adopted democracy. Challenges include corruption, wealth disparity, excessive control by a few, erosion of the judiciary's independence and manipulation of information channels.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about why the Constitution-makers adopted the parliamentary system:

1. K. T. Shah favoured the adoption of the presidential system in the Constituent Assembly.
2. K. M. Munshi argued that constitutional traditions in India had become parliamentary, so there was no reason to go back and buy a novel experience.
3. The nature of Indian society, one of the most heterogeneous and complex plural societies, favoured a system that gives scope for representation of various sections, interests and regions.
4. The framers thought that an infant democracy could afford a perpetual feud between the legislature and the executive, as in the USA.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: K. T. Shah favoured the presidential system. Statement 2 is correct: Munshi argued that India's constitutional traditions had become parliamentary. Statement 3 is correct: a plural society needed representation of various sections and regions. Statement 4 is incorrect: the framers wanted to avoid the legislative-executive conflicts bound to occur in the presidential system, as an infant democracy could not afford the risk of a perpetual feud.
w: '2, 3 and 4 only' includes statement 4, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 1, which is correct.
'1, 3 and 4 only' includes statement 4, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 2, which is correct.
